results.decision_basis: Direct original field observations from eight locations in Pakistan’s Swat River; adequate scholarly publication identity and direct biodiversity connection. Keep the descriptive fisheries evidence while rejecting strong causal interpretation of flood-attributable losses without comparable controlled monitoring.

source_verification.basis: University of Sindh Journal of Animal Sciences Vol.10(1), pp.74–85, 2026; article DOI, title, authors and full 12-page PDF checked on university-hosted journal. Methods describe sampling at eight named Swat River locations in February/March 2018 and November/December 2022, species identification using keys and pre/post questionnaires. PASTIC journal aggregation independently confirms bibliographic identity, but republishes the same abstract rather than independently replicating outcomes. University journal posting dates differ: article metadata shows 2026-06-24, PDF and PASTIC list publication 2026-06-30. No substantiated propaganda, retraction or source-laundering indicator found. Caution: 2018 is already after the 2010 flood; comparison cannot independently isolate a 2010 effect, and relative abundances/catch-per-fisher are not a standardized causal population census.

aboutness.basis: The study sampled fish at Madyan, Khwaza Khela, Matta, Ningolai, Kanju, Panjigram, Landaki and Chakdara on the Swat River, Pakistan, and compared 2018 and 2022 catches/observations. This is the actual study geography, not an institutional-address inference.
aboutness.verified_excerpt: The Methods section names eight Swat River sampling sites and 2018 versus 2022 sampling; Results describe 17 fish species and changes in observed abundance.

topic.label: Biodiversity
topic.basis: Original fish assemblage observations, species presence/absence and reported changes in relative abundance are directly biodiversity research.

futures.mechanism: Freshwater fish biodiversity surveys, standardization of long-term monitoring stations and eDNA/field-observation data infrastructure; fisheries management and flood-ecology evidence in the Swat basin.
futures.why_could_matter: If standardized repeat surveys confirm substantial changes, Pakistan’s river-conservation research and fisheries agencies could prioritize persistent monitoring, habitat restoration experiments and data-sharing tools. Such R&I implications are conditional and not demonstrated impacts of this article.
futures.uncertainty: Reported 42–51% decline mixes two distinct metrics: a ~50.54% change in a species-abundance mean (2018 vs 2022) and ~42% decline in fishermen’s reported daily catch; comparability, effort, seasonal variation, and attribution to either the 2010 or 2022 flood remain unresolved. Independent surveys in the area use different sites and species counts; they corroborate relevance, not this numerical estimate.
futures.research_question: Would standardized multi-season fish and environmental monitoring across the eight Swat River sites confirm persistent post-flood assemblage changes and identify their drivers?

results.review_reason: Final deep-or-drop resolution: DROP from the verified radar for insufficient accessible evidence, not for false geographic relevance or suspected misconduct. The chapter is traceable bibliographically (DOI, authors, IGI Global book, chapter 7, pp. 201–224), and its author-side abstract explicitly discusses Morocco, but the publisher DOI/chapter full text could not be inspected; ResearchGate explicitly offers only a request-full-text option. The EurekaMag listing repeats chapter-level summary material and confirms citation identity rather than providing independently inspectable methodology. Two separate Moroccan supply-chain studies involving Boulitama and Sabiri (a 151-firm survey published by Vilnius University Press in 2026, and a 234-firm survey published in Polish Journal of Management Studies in 2025) corroborate that the researchers study Morocco-specific digital supply chains, but they are different publications with overlapping authors, not independent verification of this chapter’s analysis or asserted digital-technology effects. No independently tested chapter-specific Moroccan rollout, sustainability result, blockchain implementation or evidence protocol was available. The user requested definitive keep/drop; the chapter does not pass the full-text/substantive-method gate for Keep, so it is excluded as unverified, with no allegation of fabrication or influence activity.
results.decision_basis: DROP — Morocco and supply chains clearly match the abstract, but verified bibliographic identity and same-author adjacent empirical research cannot substitute for examination of this specific conceptual chapter and its evidence base. Insufficient chapter-level verification for promotion to the verified radar.

source_verification.basis: ResearchGate record names Boulitama and Sabiri, IGI Global edited book AI, Blockchain, and Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Supply Chains (2026), chapter 7, pp.201–224, and the exact DOI; an independent bibliography index lists the same title and pagination, while bookseller catalogues confirm the edited book and July 16 release. The fuller book-chapter title includes “Case of Morocco”, whereas the manifest title omits this subtitle. The accessible abstract claims a structured synthesis and Morocco-grounded logistic/industrial constraints, but ResearchGate explicitly says no full text is available; the DOI redirects to inaccessible services.igi-global.com. No unsupported claim of having read the chapter or observed effects is made. Final deeper verification (2026-11-16): IGI Global DOI resolution/full chapter remained inaccessible for chapter-level methodology review. A 2026 Vilnius University Press article by Boulitama and Sabiri, DOI 10.15388/Ekon.2026.105.1.3, reports a 151-firm Moroccan survey; a 2025 Polish Journal of Management Studies paper by Boulitama and Sabiri, DOI 10.17512/pjms.2025.32.1.04, reports a 234-company mixed-mode Moroccan survey. These are primary scholarly studies of closely related topics, but not independent validation of the chapter: they partly share the chapter authors and do not supply the missing chapter text or separate ESG/blockchain impact evidence. Source identity and relevance are supported, but chapter-specific research integrity and strength of evidence remain unverified. The Drop is exclusion on an evidence-threshold basis, not an accusation of illegitimacy.

aboutness.basis: The accessible chapter abstract explicitly offers a Morocco-grounded account of logistics, industrial constraints, data interoperability, organizational capacity and SME inclusion; this is more than an author affiliation. Full chapter case evidence was not inspected.
aboutness.verified_excerpt: The available chapter abstract describes Morocco-grounded logistics and industrial constraints and a staged pathway from data readiness to AI decision use and selective blockchain traceability.

topic.label: Supply chains
topic.basis: Supply-chain visibility, data governance, AI-supported forecasting, traceability and inter-firm interoperability are the central objects of the abstract.

futures.mechanism: Moroccan supply-chain interoperability and data-governance standards; skills for logistics AI; cross-firm traceability and audit evidence; SME participation in shared digital infrastructures.
futures.why_could_matter: If the proposed data-governance and AI implementations are tested with Moroccan industrial and logistics partners, they could create applied research testbeds and skills partnerships. This is a research possibility inferred from the abstract, not an observed rollout.
futures.uncertainty: The accessible record provides a conceptual synthesis, not independently validated Moroccan case-study results, implementation counts, baseline outcomes or demonstrated cost/emissions reductions. Whether the publisher manuscript supports more specific country claims is unresolved. This chapter was dropped from the verified collection; related Morocco studies could be independently screened as separate candidate records, not silently substituted under this ID.
futures.research_question: What interoperability, data-quality and workforce conditions would allow independently evaluated AI-and-traceability pilots to improve Moroccan supply-chain performance?

results.review_reason: Final deep-or-drop resolution: DROP from the verified radar on methodological quality, not because the subject or Albanian geography is irrelevant. The full 7-page publisher PDF was inspected including p.69 research methodology, p.70 readiness pie chart and p.71 ESG impact graph. The paper describes its 15%/45%/40% technology-provider segments as adapted from Tavanxhiu et al. (2026) but does not give a fresh sample, denominator, or audit trail for converting the original 17.7%/43.5%/38.8% in Godolja et al. (2025) into these figures. The paper’s expert-derived potential scores (7.5–9.2 on a 0–10 scale) do not disclose number or selection of experts, questions, weighting, calibration, or uncertainty estimates. Its own limitations concede reliance on general assessments instead of comprehensive original data for readiness, and the broad benefits asserted are scenario/technology potentials rather than measured Albanian hotel outcomes. Publisher article and PDF date the publication June 30, 2026, rather than manifest June 1, 2026. An independent peer-reviewed 2025 provider study with N=1,821 validates a broad Albania-specific readiness challenge, not this manuscript’s reworked figures or AI-ESG scores. No plagiarism/fabrication/propaganda allegation is made; the candidate is excluded because its prominent quantitative findings cannot be validated to the radar standard.
results.decision_basis: DROP — authentic Albania-specific AI-tourism article, but derivative sector-readiness percentages and un-auditable expert ESG scores are central to its results; they do not meet the verification standard. Prefer the separate 2025 primary provider survey as a new, distinct candidate.

source_verification.basis: The European Journal of Business and Management (IISTE) article DOI, authors, 7-page PDF and Albanian sector focus match the record. The manifest supplies 2026-06-01 but journal page and PDF both print June 30, 2026. The article says its readiness segments were adapted from Tavanxhiu et al. (2026) and that numerical ESG potential scores are expert-derived; it also admits segments are based on general assessments, not comprehensive primary survey data. The publisher openly advertises a paid peer-review process and an approximately 10-day review cycle, a quality-control concern rather than proof of fabrication. Separate primary empirical work by Godolja et al. (2025) reports N=1,821 providers and segment percentages of 17.7/43.5/38.8, similar in pattern but not identical to this article’s 15/45/40 rounding. No independent assessment of this paper’s 7.5–9.2 scores was established. Final recheck (2026-11-16): full PDF pages 69–71 inspected directly. Page 69 labels the work exploratory/descriptive, bases provider segmentation on Tavanxhiu et al. (2026) and invokes an expert-derived AI impact index without a detailed scoring method. Page 70 charts provider group shares 15.0%/45.0%/40.0%; page 71 reports 7.5–9.2 impact assessments with no auditable expert protocol or confidence intervals. The separate 2025 Tourism and Hospitality study by Godolja, Tavanxhiu and Sevrani reports N=1,821 and actual segment values 17.7%/43.5%/38.8%; it supports the broad context but not the source article’s numerical ESG claims. Drop reflects insufficient methodological evidence, not a finding that the journal is a fabricated enterprise.

aboutness.basis: The paper reviews AI adoption by Albanian accommodation providers and travel agencies and discusses national tourism sector constraints; actual Albanian hospitality research by other teams provides independent context. Place is a study object, not a publisher location.
aboutness.verified_excerpt: The Methods section builds an Albania-specific accommodation-provider readiness segmentation on existing studies; the Limitations section acknowledges the lack of a comprehensive original survey for the segmentation.

topic.label: Artificial intelligence
topic.basis: AI tools for hotel energy and waste management, service personalization and ESG data-reporting form the central topic.

futures.mechanism: Hotel/agency AI adoption research, local hospitality data infrastructures, sustainability metrics, responsible AI training and cross-enterprise field trials.
futures.why_could_matter: If validated with representative provider data, the described barriers could guide Albanian tourism-sector AI pilot research and skills development. Separately published studies already substantiate a broad adoption-readiness gap; this paper’s numerical effect estimates should not be used for planning without independent validation.
futures.uncertainty: No reproducible sample design for the paper’s displayed readiness shares; no transparent elicitation process, number of experts or uncertainty intervals for its 7.5–9.2 ESG impact index. Literature-based examples cannot establish actual national ESG improvements or rates of deployment. This candidate was dropped; it should not be cited as verified quantitative evidence for AI-ESG effects in Albania.
futures.research_question: Would a representative Albanian hotel-and-agency survey with audited energy, waste and service outcomes replicate the reported AI-readiness segments and show measurable ESG benefits?

results.decision_basis: Verified journal paper with direct primary survey observations on Pakistan’s small-business financing and start-up capital. Financial access is an entrepreneurship and potential innovation-enabling mechanism, but results concern retail SMEs in a subnational locality, not a national technology start-up ecosystem.

source_verification.basis: 17-page PDF in Journal of Business and Management Research Vol.5(1), pp.707–723, DOI and author identities align with publisher record. Methodology documents a survey of 60 completed questionnaires from 90 approached SME employees/entrepreneurs in newly merged districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, including shops/retail businesses; descriptive SPSS results are published. Pakistan Higher Education Commission’s 2024–25 national-journals PDF independently lists this exact journal, ISSNs 2958-5066 and 2958-5074, publisher Go Green Research and Education, in its Y category; historical journal recognition is not an endorsement of this article’s methodology or proof of a 2026 journal status. Journal site states an APC and a peer-review process. No substantiated retraction or influence-operation evidence found. Small and local nonrandom response, ambiguous random-sampling claim, and descriptive-only outcomes limit inference.

aboutness.basis: Study design explicitly centers SMEs in the newly merged Khyber Pakhtunkhwa districts, Pakistan, and reports primary responses from their retail entrepreneurs/enterprise employees. Findings must not be extrapolated to all Pakistani start-ups.
aboutness.verified_excerpt: The Methodology section reports 60 completed SME questionnaires from retailers such as pharmacies, clothing and mobile-phone shops in newly merged Khyber Pakhtunkhwa districts.

topic.label: Start-ups
topic.basis: Questionnaires address start-up capital, original sources of funding, difficulties obtaining credit and collateral, and early firm growth. It is about business start-ups broadly, not specifically research-intensive ventures.

futures.mechanism: Access to seed capital, SME finance literacy and collateral rules as enabling or constraining conditions for business experimentation, technology uptake and local entrepreneurial ecosystems.
futures.why_could_matter: If funding and information barriers observed among sampled SMEs are confirmed for new innovation-oriented enterprises, Pakistan’s entrepreneurial support and applied research partnerships could test alternative credit-information, training or seed-funding models. Such effects were not tested by this study.
futures.uncertainty: Only 60 respondents within newly merged districts, predominantly retailers; the paper lacks a technology-start-up subgroup, validated finance intervention, causal design, or innovation-output data. Reported shares should be treated as sample descriptives, not national prevalence.
futures.research_question: Do financing-information and collateral barriers identified among small Pakistani retailers also constrain the formation and innovation activity of technology-oriented start-ups, and which pilot support measures help?

results.decision_basis: Substantive Albanian parliamentary AI policy/administration case study based partly on a named April 2025 interview; its specific AI transcription procurement context is supported by independent procurement reporting. Treat improvements as proposed/claimed, not demonstrated.

source_verification.basis: Albanian University Optime Vol.17(1), pp.267–271, publication 2025-06-01, author Erjon Dervishi and exact DOI verified against university journal record and 5-page PDF. The paper cites an interview of Albanian Parliament IT Director Dritan Kaloshi conducted 2025-04-09, describes a contemplated Whisper-style transcription procurement, existing E-Parliament/parliamentary research functions and AI governance issues. Separate February and June 2025 Albanian media reports cite an actual tender and then the award for an AI-assisted transcription system; these are independent corroboration of procurement occurrence, not demonstrated transcription accuracy, operational speed or accessibility impact. Optime is explicitly the scientific journal of Albanian University; no substantiated deceptive publishing or propaganda operation found.

aboutness.basis: The empirical case is the Albanian Parliament’s own IT services, transcription workflow, procurement and legislative governance, supported by a direct interview and named institutional arrangements. Country relevance is the studied system, not an affiliation.
aboutness.verified_excerpt: The full text describes Parliament considering AI speech-to-text transcription of committee and plenary audio and attributes the procurement discussion to an April 9, 2025 interview with its IT director.

topic.label: Artificial intelligence
topic.basis: Direct case study of AI-assisted parliamentary transcription, organizational adoption, public-sector AI policy and oversight.

futures.mechanism: Albanian-language automatic speech recognition and document pipelines, parliamentary data access, human-review protocols, algorithmic quality assessment, and public-sector AI skills/procurement research.
futures.why_could_matter: If the transcription system is implemented with transparent quality tests and human review, parliamentary audio could be converted into reusable, accessible research and legislative records, creating opportunities for Albanian-language speech technology evaluation. Procurement reporting demonstrates activity, not that the claimed quality/turnaround gains were achieved.
futures.uncertainty: Paper discusses planned, not evaluated, AI deployment; advertised 20-minute editing estimates are not independently measured; transcript error rates, bilingual/dialect performance, security, oversight, real deployment status and contract changes require checks. 2025 award media and 2026 procurement material should not be automatically assumed to describe identical work packages.
futures.research_question: How accurately and accessibly could Albanian Parliament speech-to-text systems capture plenary/committee proceedings under independently measured Albanian-language error, cost and human-oversight benchmarks?
